doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Philadelphia, the late bus and first days with the Chief
summary: Waiting for cymbals by Greyhound, Robin Hood Dell with Arthur Prysock, oversleeping, and stories with Basie.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I stopped Vic Damone’s rehearsal, and took his drummer’s sticks and brushes and cymbals and ten minutes later I was swinging the Basie band. I will never forget that. And the next night we were playing in a place called the Robin Hood Dell, it’s a big amphitheater in Philadelphia. And we bussed it from New York and went to Philly and everything. Now I unfortunately had to wait, they couldn’t stop in New York to get my cymbals, but they put my cymbals on a bus, on a Greyhound, to Philadelphia, and Count Basie himself and the whole band waited on the bus for close to 45 minutes while I went downtown to the bus station, got caught in a big traffic jam in a cab, it cost like $50 in a cab, to get my cymbals. And when I got on the bus, I looked at Basie and I said, “Sorry, Count,” you know I called him “The Chief” you know everybody called him “The Chief.” I said, “Sorry, Chief, you know I’ll try not to make this a habit.” So we go and we play the gig and it was with Arthur Prysock and everything, I mean 25,000 people and they were swinging, you know, groovin’. The next day we played a little country club gig, and by that time I was so exhausted, I didn’t even know what day it was. And all of a sudden the phone rings, and I was like twenty minutes late getting on the bus. And you know I said, “Oh I’ll be down in a minute.” And all my stuff was all unpacked, all over the room. I packed in less than three minutes, was on the bus, and I looked at the Chief and I said, “I don’t know what to tell you.” But then I went out and I bought a clock and a watch and everything, you know. But my first 72 hours on the band were a little strange there. But Chief really had a lot of compassion and he permitted me to just get in sync with the rest of the band, and it took a few days but I was just really loving his spirit so much every night. And just looking at him and traveling with him every day and everything, and you know I tried not to bother him too much you know, but every once in a while he’d say, “Hey Duffy come on over here,” and I’d sit and he’d tell me some stories and stuff.
